summary: Guardian Australia profiles Vincent Namatjira, the 40-year-old Western Arrernte artist known for colourful, satirical portraits that both skewer and honour their subjects, often with himself painted in. Taken from his family as a child and raised in foster care in Perth, he returned to central Australia at 18 and later built a prize-winning career while stepping out of the shadow of his great-grandfather Albert Namatjira. The piece covers his work, his views on colonialism, power and the royals, and the upcoming Australia in Colour survey exhibition and monograph.
one_line: Artist Vincent Namatjira discusses satire, colonialism, foster care and carving his own path beyond his great-grandfather Albert Namatjira's legacy ahead of his Australia in Colour exhibition.
key_facts: Vincent Namatjira, now 40, won his first prize as a teenager in Perth for drawing a replica of HMS Endeavour, the ship that delivered James Cook to Dharawal country in 1770.
He won the Ramsay art prize in 2019 with a Cook-inspired work and the Archibald Prize in 2020 with a portrait of AFL footballer Adam Goodes titled Stand Strong for Who You Are.
He has also been awarded an Order of Australia medal.
Namatjira was born in Alice Springs in 1983 and, after his mother Jillian Namatjira's death, was moved to Perth with his sister and placed in foster care.
At 18 he returned to central Australia and was met by many crying relatives who knew him only through his mother's name; he settled in Indulkana in the APY lands.

His great-grandfather Albert Namatjira (1902-59) was a famous western Arrernte watercolour landscape painter of the Hermannsburg school; Vincent never met him and did not know of the connection as a teenager.
Vincent's work featuring his great-grandfather includes the 13-panel series Albert's Story (2014) and a 2023 portrait in the Desert Songs series.
His 2016 series Prime Ministers depicts the seven Australian leaders of his lifetime, and 2018's Vincent & Donald (Happy Birthday) shows him sharing a cake with Trump; both were born on 14 June.
He says painting the queen or king on country is 'like taking away their power' and that 'I see myself as a royal', recasting Albert's 1954 handshake with Queen Elizabeth II as an equalising moment.
He says he would like the government to apologise for taking Indigenous children into foster care.
Vincent Namatjira: Australia in Colour opens on 20 October at the Art Gallery of South Australia as part of Tarnanthi festival, before touring nationally.
Desert Songs shows until 28 October at Yavuz Gallery in Surry Hills, Sydney, and the monograph Vincent Namatjira (Thames & Hudson) is out now.
He paints in his studio at Iwantja Arts in Indulkana, and says of his legacy: 'He chose his own path. Well, I choose mine.'
